name: Aminata Diallo
headline: 19-year-old apprentice bricklayer and part-time student, Bamako, Mali
title: The Weekly Count
situation: At the end of the day, as the crew packs up, Sékou walks over to Aminata. The site manager needs someone to stay an extra hour tonight to do the weekly inventory count before the next delivery arrives in the morning. The manager is about to leave, so Sékou says, 'Decide now, little comptable. Do you take it?' There is no overtime pay, only the responsibility. Aminata has her accounting notebook waiting at home and a long walk back. She has to answer before Sékou turns to leave.

context.relationship_profiles:
Sékou has trained her for two years, trusts her numbers, and treats her like a protégée but never offers favors.
The site manager barely knows her name and only sees her as a reliable extra hand.
context.tendencies:
She routinely stays late to double-check measurements even without pay.
She has never asked for an advance on her wage.
When faced with unexpected requests, she first calculates the cost in time and then answers.
context.current_state:
She is physically exhausted after ten hours of hauling cement, her eyes burn from dust, and she has a two-hour walk ahead if she leaves now.
Her accounting notebook is at home, and tonight's study session is already shortened.
context.immediate_memories:
The phrase 'weekly count' pulls her back to the last inventory, where she was the only one who noticed the cement bags on the delivery sheet didn't match the pile.
The site manager's hurried tone reminds her of the time her mother's loan was called in without warning.
context.reflective_memories:
She remembers her mother losing the stall because someone else's arithmetic was trusted over hers.
She also remembers the nights she walked home after extra hours, counting steps to keep herself awake, and how those hours built the savings under the floorboard.
